claim: Homo naledi is a previously-unknown species of extinct hominin discovered within the Dinaledi Chamber of the Rising Star cave system, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa.
source: Homo naledi is a previously-unknown species of extinct hominin discovered within the Dinaledi Chamber of the Rising Star cave system, Cradle of Humankind, South Africa.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the discovery and location of the new species.

claim: Homo naledi is characterized by body mass and stature similar to small-bodied human populations.
source: This species is characterized by body mass and stature similar to small-bodied human populations but a small endocranial volume similar to australopiths.
evidence: Body mass estimates from femoral specimens and stature estimates from tibia length are provided in the manuscript.

claim: Homo naledi has a small endocranial volume similar to australopiths.
source: This species is characterized by body mass and stature similar to small-bodied human populations but a small endocranial volume similar to australopiths.
evidence: Endocranial volume estimates of approximately 560cc and 465cc are provided, which overlap with australopith ranges.

claim: Cranial morphology of H. naledi is unique, but most similar to early Homo species including Homo erectus, Homo habilis or Homo rudolfensis.
source: Cranial morphology of H. naledi is unique, but most similar to early Homo species including Homo erectus, Homo habilis or Homo rudolfensis.
evidence: Comparative morphological analysis is provided in the differential diagnosis section.

claim: The dentition of H. naledi is generally small and simple in occlusal morphology.
source: While primitive, the dentition is generally small and simple in occlusal morphology.
evidence: Dental measurements and morphological descriptions are provided in the manuscript.

claim: H. naledi has humanlike manipulatory adaptations of the hand and wrist.
source: H. naledi has humanlike manipulatory adaptations of the hand and wrist.
evidence: Detailed descriptions of hand and wrist morphology are provided, including comparisons to other hominins.

claim: H. naledi exhibits a humanlike foot and lower limb.
source: It also exhibits a humanlike foot and lower limb.
evidence: Detailed descriptions of foot and lower limb morphology are provided in the manuscript.

claim: H. naledi has a more primitive or australopith-like trunk, shoulder, pelvis and proximal femur.
source: These humanlike aspects are contrasted in the postcrania with a more primitive or australopith-like trunk, shoulder, pelvis and proximal femur.
evidence: Morphological descriptions of these anatomical regions are provided in the manuscript.

claim: The Dinaledi collection represents at least 15 individuals.
source: Representing at least 15 individuals with most skeletal elements repeated multiple times, this is the largest assemblage of a single species of hominins yet discovered in Africa.
evidence: The minimum number of individuals is determined by repetition and presence of deciduous and adult dental elements.

claim: The Dinaledi collection is the largest assemblage of a single species of hominins yet discovered in Africa.
source: Representing at least 15 individuals with most skeletal elements repeated multiple times, this is the largest assemblage of a single species of hominins yet discovered in Africa.
evidence: The collection comprises 1550 fossil hominin specimens with nearly every skeletal element represented multiple times.

claim: Fossil hominins were first recognized in the Dinaledi Chamber in October 2013.
source: Fossil hominins were first recognized in the Dinaledi Chamber in the Rising Star cave system in October 2013.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of the discovery.

claim: The team recovered 1550 hominin specimens during excavation.
source: During a relatively short excavation, our team recovered an extensive collection of 1550 hominin specimens, representing nearly every element of the skeleton multiple times (Figure 1), including many complete elements and morphologically informative fragments, some in articulation, as well as smaller fragments many of which could be refit into more complete elements.
evidence: The number of specimens is explicitly stated and documented.

claim: The Dinaledi collection is a morphologically homogeneous sample.
source: The collection is a morphologically homogeneous sample that can be attributed to no previously-known hominin species.
evidence: Morphological homogeneity is demonstrated through comparative analysis and variation assessment.

claim: The word naledi means 'star' in the Sotho language.
source: The word naledi means 'star' in the Sotho language and refers to the Dinaledi Chamber's location within the Rising Star cave system.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the etymology of the species name.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber is located approximately 30 meters underground.
source: The Dinaledi chamber is located approximately 30 meters underground, within the Rising Star cave system at about 26°1′13′′ S; 27°42′43′′ E.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the location and depth of the chamber.

claim: The Rising Star cave system lies within the Malmani dolomites, approximately 800 meters southwest of Swartkrans.
source: The system lies within the Malmani dolomites, approximately 800 meters southwest of the well-known site of Swartkrans in the Cradle of Humankind World Heritage Site, Gauteng Province, South Africa.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the geological and geographic location.

claim: The present sample of skeletal material from the Dinaledi Chamber was recovered during two field expeditions, in November 2013 and March 2014.
source: The present sample of skeletal material from the Dinaledi Chamber was recovered during two field expeditions, in November 2013 and March 2014.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of excavations.

claim: Six specimens from an ex situ context can be identified as bird bones.
source: Six specimens from an ex situ context can be identified as bird bones, and few fragmentary rodent remains have been recovered within the excavation area. Neither of these faunal constituents can presently be associated with the hominin fossil collection (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about non-hominin faunal remains, with citation to supporting work.

claim: The Dinaledi collection comprises 1550 fossil hominin specimens, including 1413 bone specimens and 137 isolated dental specimens.
source: The collection so far comprises 1550 fossil hominin specimens, this number includes 1413 bone specimens and 137 isolated dental specimens; an additional 53 teeth are present in mandibular or maxillary bone specimens.
evidence: This is a direct statement providing specific counts of specimens.

claim: All dental crowns (n = 179) in the collection are hominin.
source: Aside from the fragmentary rodent teeth, all dental crowns (n = 179) are hominin, recovered both from surface collection and excavation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic identification of dental remains.

claim: All morphologically informative bone specimens are clearly hominin.
source: Likewise, aside from the few bird elements, all morphologically informative bone specimens are clearly hominin.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic identification of bone specimens.

claim: The remains are morphologically homogeneous, with variation consistent with body size and sex differences within a single population.
source: In all cases where elements are repeated in the sample, they are morphologically homogeneous, with variation consistent with body size and sex differences within a single population.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the morphological variation in the sample.

claim: The geological age of the fossils is not yet known.
source: The geological age of the fossils is not yet known.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of dating information.

claim: Excavations have recovered hominin material from Unit 2 and Unit 3 in the chamber.
source: Excavations have thus far recovered hominin material from Unit 2 and Unit 3 in the chamber (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stratigraphic context, with citation to supporting work.

claim: Surface-collected hominin material is morphologically indistinguishable from material excavated from in situ within Unit 3.
source: Surface-collected hominin material from the present top of Unit 3, which includes material derived from both Unit 2 and Unit 3, represents a minority of the assemblage, and is morphologically indistinguishable from material excavated from in situ within Unit 3.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the morphological similarity of surface and excavated materials.

claim: Distinctive morphological configurations of all the recovered first metacarpals, femora, molars, lower premolars and lower canines are identical in both surface-collected and excavated specimens.
source: In addition to general morphological homogeneity including cranial shape, distinctive morphological configurations of all the recovered first metacarpals, femora, molars, lower premolars and lower canines, are identical in both surface-collected and excavated specimens (see Figure 14 later in the text).
evidence: This statement is supported by morphological analysis and reference to Figure 14.

claim: The distinctive morphological traits found in H. naledi specimens are not found in any other hominin species yet described.
source: These include traits not found in any other hominin species yet described.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with other hominin species.

claim: The material represents a single species, and not a commingled assemblage.
source: These considerations strongly indicate that this material represents a single species, and not a commingled assemblage.
evidence: This conclusion is based on morphological homogeneity and distinctive shared traits.

claim: The holotype DH1 is a presumed male individual, based on size and morphology within the sample.
source: Dinaledi Hominin 1 (DH1) comprises the partial calvaria, partial maxilla, and nearly complete mandible of a presumed male individual, based on size and morphology within the sample (Figure 2; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Sex determination is based on comparative size and morphology within the sample.

claim: The holotype was recovered in situ during excavations within the Dinaledi Chamber in March of 2014.
source: The holotype was recovered in situ during excavations within the Dinaledi Chamber in March of 2014, embedded in unconsolidated fine clay matrix (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recovery context, with citation to supporting work.

claim: DH3 is a partial calvaria of a presumed female individual.
source: Dinaledi Hominin 3 (DH3) is a partial calvaria of a presumed female individual that preserves parts of the frontal, left parietal, left temporal, and sphenoid (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Sex determination is based on comparative size and morphology within the sample.

claim: The cranial specimens agree closely in nearly all morphological details where they overlap except those interpreted as related to sex.
source: These cranial specimens agree closely in nearly all morphological details where they overlap in areas preserved except those we interpret as related to sex.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis of the cranial specimens.

claim: Dinaledi hand 1 (H1) is a nearly complete right hand, found articulated in association.
source: Dinaledi hand 1 (H1) is a nearly complete (missing only the pisiform) right hand, found articulated in association, comprising specimens U.W. 101-1308 to −1311, −1318 to −1321, −1325 to −1329, −1351, −1464, and −1721 to −1732 (Figure 6; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the discovery and composition of the hand specimen.

claim: Dinaledi foot 1 (F1) is a partial foot skeleton missing only the medial cuneiform and the phalanges of rays II–V.
source: Dinaledi foot 1 (F1) is a partial foot skeleton missing only the medial cuneiform and the phalanges of rays II–V.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the composition of the foot specimen.

claim: The holotypes, paratypes and referred material comprise 737 partial or complete anatomical elements.
source: We refer to H. naledi all hominin material from the Dinaledi collection that can be identified to element; in total, the holotypes, paratypes and referred material comprise 737 partial or complete anatomical elements.
evidence: This is a direct statement providing a count of anatomical elements.

claim: The cranium of H. naledi does not have the well-developed crest patterns that characterize Australopithecus garhi and species of the genus Paranthropus.
source: The cranium of H. naledi does not have the well-developed crest patterns that characterize Australopithecus garhi (Asfaw et al., 1999) and species of the genus Paranthropus, nor the derived facial morphology seen in the latter genus.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with citation to supporting work.

claim: The mandible of H. naledi is notably more gracile than those of Paranthropus.
source: The mandible of H. naledi is notably more gracile than those of Paranthropus.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The post-canine teeth of H. naledi are notably smaller than those of Paranthropus and Au. garhi.
source: Although maxillary and mandibular incisors and canines of H. naledi overlap in size with those of Paranthropus, the post-canine teeth are notably smaller than those of Paranthropus and Au. garhi, with mandibular molars that are buccolingually narrow.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: H. naledi differs from Australopithecus afarensis and Australopithecus africanus in having a pentagonal-shaped cranial vault in posterior view.
source: H. naledi differs from Australopithecus afarensis and Australopithecus africanus in having a pentagonal-shaped cranial vault in posterior view, sagittal keeling, widely spaced temporal lines, an angular torus, a deep and narrow digastric fossa, an external occipital protuberance, an anteriorly positioned root of the zygomatic process of the maxilla, a broad palate, and a small canine jugum lacking anterior pillars.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The H. naledi mandible exhibits a more gracile symphysis and corpus than Au. afarensis and Au. africanus.
source: The H. naledi mandible exhibits a more gracile symphysis and corpus, a more vertically inclined symphysis, a slight mandibular incurvation delineating a faint mental trigon, and a steeply inclined posterior face of the mandibular symphysis without a post incisive planum.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The incisors of H. naledi overlap in size with some specimens of Au. africanus.
source: The incisors of H. naledi overlap in size with some specimens of Au. africanus, though the canines and post-canine dentition are notably smaller, with relatively narrow buccolingual dimensions of the mandibular molars.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: H. naledi exhibits a small and isolated Carabelli's feature in the maxillary molars, unlike the more prominent and extensive Carabelli's feature of Australopithecus.
source: H. naledi exhibits a small and isolated Carabelli's feature in the maxillary molars, unlike the more prominent and extensive Carabelli's feature of Australopithecus.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental morphology.

claim: The H. naledi mandibular molars possess small, mesiobuccally restricted protostylids that do not intersect the buccal groove, differing from Australopithecus.
source: Moreover, the H. naledi mandibular molars possess small, mesiobuccally restricted protostylids that do not intersect the buccal groove, differing from the typically enlarged, centrally positioned protostylids that intersect the buccal groove in Australopithecus.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental morphology.

claim: The cranium of H. naledi differs from Australopithecus sediba in exhibiting sagittal keeling.
source: The cranium of H. naledi differs from Australopithecus sediba (Berger et al., 2010) in exhibiting sagittal keeling, a more pronounced supraorbital torus and supratoral sulcus, a weakly arched supraorbital contour with rounded lateral corners, an angular torus, a well-defined supramastoid crest, a curved superior margin of the temporal squama, a root of the zygomatic process of the temporal that is angled downwards approximately 30° relative to FH, a flattened nasoalveolar clivus, weak canine juga, an anteriorly positioned root of the zygomatic process of the maxilla, and a relatively broad palate that is anteriorly shallow.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with citation to supporting work.

claim: The maxillary and mandibular teeth of H. naledi are smaller than those of Au. sediba.
source: The maxillary and mandibular teeth of H. naledi are smaller than those of Au. sediba, with mandibular molars that are buccolingually narrow.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: The cranium of H. naledi differs from Homo habilis in exhibiting sagittal keeling.
source: The cranium of H. naledi differs from Homo habilis in exhibiting sagittal keeling, a weakly arched supraorbital contour, temporal lines that are positioned on the posterior rather than the superior aspect of the supraorbital torus, an angular torus, an occipital torus, only slight post-orbital constriction, a curved superior margin of the temporal squama, a suprameatal spine, a weak crista petrosa, a prominent Eustachian process, a small EAM, weak canine juga, and an anteriorly positioned root of the zygomatic process of the maxilla.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The maxillary and mandibular dentitions of DH1 are smaller than typical for H. habilis.
source: The maxillary and mandibular dentitions of DH1 are smaller than typical for H. habilis.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: The mandibular P3 of H. naledi is more molarized and lacks the occlusal simplification seen in H. habilis.
source: The mandibular P3 of H. naledi is more molarized and lacks the occlusal simplification seen in H. habilis; it has a symmetrical occlusal outline, and multiple roots (two roots: mesiobuccal and distal) not seen in H. habilis.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental morphology.

claim: The molars of H. naledi lack crenulation, secondary fissures, and supernumerary cusps that are common to H. habilis.
source: The molars of H. naledi lack crenulation, secondary fissures, and supernumerary cusps that are common to H. habilis.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental morphology.

claim: The cranium of H. naledi differs from Homo rudolfensis by its smaller cranial capacity.
source: The cranium of H. naledi differs from Homo rudolfensis by its smaller cranial capacity, and by exhibiting frontal bossing, a post-bregmatic depression, sagittal keeling, a well-developed supraorbital torus delineated by a distinct supratoral sulcus, temporal lines that are positioned on the posterior rather than the superior aspect of the supraorbital torus, an occipital torus, an external occipital protuberance, only slight post-orbital constriction, a small postglenoid process, a weak crista petrosa, a laterally inflated mastoid process, a canine fossa, incisors that project anteriorly beyond the bi-canine line, and a shallow anterior palate.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis and cranial capacity estimates.

claim: The maxillary and mandibular dentition of H. naledi is smaller than that of most specimens of H. rudolfensis.
source: The maxillary and mandibular dentition of H. naledi is smaller than that of most specimens of H. rudolfensis, with only KNM-ER 60000 and KNM-ER 62000 appearing similar in size for some teeth (Leakey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements with citation to supporting work.

claim: H. naledi lacks the typically distinctive long and low cranial vault of Homo erectus.
source: H. naledi lacks the typically distinctive long and low cranial vault of Homo erectus, as well as the metopic keeling that is typically present in the latter species.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The maxillary and mandibular incisors and canines of H. naledi are smaller than typical of H. erectus.
source: The maxillary and mandibular incisors and canines of H. naledi are smaller than typical of H. erectus.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: H. naledi lacks the reduced cranial height of Homo floresiensis.
source: H. naledi lacks the reduced cranial height of Homo floresiensis, and displays a marked angular torus and parasagittal keeling between bregma and lambda that is absent in the latter species.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: H. naledi is distinguishable from H. floresiensis by the mesiodistal elongation and extensive talonid of the mandibular P4.
source: Dentally, H. naledi is distinguishable from H. floresiensis by the mesiodistal elongation and extensive talonid of the mandibular P4, and the lack of Tomes' root on the mandibular premolars.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental morphology.

claim: The molar size gradient of H. naledi follows the M1 < M2 < M3 pattern, unlike the M3 < M2 < M1 pattern in H. floresiensis.
source: The molar size gradient of H. naledi follows the M1 < M2 < M3 pattern, unlike the M3 < M2 < M1 pattern in H. floresiensis, and the mandibular molars are relatively mesiodistally long and buccolingually narrow compared to those of H. floresiensis.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: H. naledi differs from Middle Pleistocene and Late Pleistocene Homo in exhibiting a smaller cranial capacity.
source: H. naledi differs from Middle Pleistocene (MP) and Late Pleistocene (LP) Homo (here we include specimens sometimes attributed to the putative Early Pleistocene taxon Homo antecessor, and MP Homo heidelbergensis, Homo rhodesiensis, as well as archaic Homo sapiens and Neandertals) in exhibiting a smaller cranial capacity.
evidence: This is based on comparative cranial capacity estimates.

claim: H. naledi has its maximum cranial width in the supramastoid region, rather than in the parietal region.
source: H. naledi has its maximum cranial width in the supramastoid region, rather than in the parietal region.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of cranial specimens.

claim: H. naledi lacks the bilaterally arched and vertically thickened supraorbital tori found in MP and LP Homo.
source: H. naledi lacks the bilaterally arched and vertically thickened supraorbital tori found in MP and LP Homo.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The mandibular canine of H. naledi retains a distinct accessory distal cuspulid not seen in MP and LP Homo.
source: The mandibular canine retains a distinct accessory distal cuspulid not seen in MP and LP Homo.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental morphology.

claim: Molar cuspal proportions for H. naledi do not show the derived reduction of the entoconid and hypoconid that characterizes MP and LP Homo.
source: Molar cuspal proportions for H. naledi do not show the derived reduction of the entoconid and hypoconid that characterizes MP and LP Homo.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental morphology.

claim: The mandibular M3 is not reduced in DH1, revealing an increasing molar size gradient that contrasts with reduction of the M3 in MP and LP Homo.
source: The mandibular M3 is not reduced in DH1, thus revealing an increasing molar size gradient that contrasts with reduction of the M3 in MP and LP Homo.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: H. naledi differs from H. sapiens in exhibiting small cranial capacity.
source: H. naledi differs from H. sapiens in exhibiting small cranial capacity, a well-defined supraorbital torus and supratoral sulcus, a root of the zygomatic process of the temporal that is angled downwards approximately 30° relative to FH, a large and laterally inflated mastoid with well-developed supramastoid crest, an angular torus, a small vaginal process, a weak crista petrosa, a prominent Eustachian process, a small EAM, a flat and squared nasoalveolar clivus, and a more posteriorly positioned incisive foramen.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis and cranial capacity estimates.

claim: The H. naledi mandible shows a weaker, less well-defined mentum osseum than H. sapiens.
source: The H. naledi mandible shows a weaker, less well-defined mentum osseum than H. sapiens, as well as a slight inferior transverse torus that is absent in humans.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: H1 is differentiated from the estimated intrinsic hand proportions of Au. afarensis in having a relatively long thumb.
source: H1 is differentiated from the estimated intrinsic hand proportions of Au. afarensis in having a relatively long thumb ((Mc1 + PP1)/(Mc3 + PP3 + IP3)) (Rolian and Gordon, 2013; Almécija and Alba, 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphometric analysis with citations to supporting work.

claim: H1 is distinguished from Au. afarensis, Au. africanus, and Au. sediba in having a well-developed crest for both the opponens pollicis and first dorsal interosseous muscles.
source: It is further distinguished from Au. afarensis, Au. africanus, and Au. sediba in having a well-developed crest for both the opponens pollicis and first dorsal interosseous muscles, a trapezium-scaphoid joint that extends onto the scaphoid tubercle, a relatively large and more palmarly-positioned capitate-trapezoid joint, and/or a saddle-shaped Mc5-hamate joint.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: H1 is distinguished from H. habilis in having a deep proximal palmar fossa with a well-developed ridge distally for the insertion of the flexor pollicis longus muscle on the first distal phalanx.
source: H1 is distinguished from H. habilis in having a deep proximal palmar fossa with a well-developed ridge distally for the insertion of the flexor pollicis longus muscle on the first distal phalanx, and a more proximodistally oriented trapezium-second metacarpal joint.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: H1 differs from both H. habilis and H. floresiensis by having a relatively large trapezium-scaphoid joint that extends onto the scaphoid tubercle.
source: It also differs from both H. habilis and H. floresiensis by having a relatively large trapezium-scaphoid joint that extends onto the scaphoid tubercle, and from H. floresiensis in having a boot-shaped trapezoid with an expanded palmar surface, and a relatively large and more palmarly-positioned capitate-trapezoid joint (Tocheri et al., 2005, 2007; Orr et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with citations to supporting work.

claim: H1 is dissimilar to hand remains attributed to Paranthropus robustus/early Homo from Swartkrans in having a relatively small Mc1 base and proximal articular facet.
source: H1 is dissimilar to hand remains attributed to Paranthropus robustus/early Homo from Swartkrans (Susman, 1988; Susman et al., 2001) in having a relatively small Mc1 base and proximal articular facet, a saddle-shaped Mc5-hamate joint, and more curved proximal and intermediate phalanges of ray 2–5.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with citations to supporting work.

claim: H1 differs from a third metacarpal attributed to H. erectus s. l., as well as from Homo neanderthalensis and H. sapiens by lacking a styloid process.
source: Manual morphology of H. rudolfensis is currently unknown, and that of H. erectus is largely unknown. Still, H1 differs from a third metacarpal attributed to H. erectus s. l., as well as from Homo neanderthalensis and H. sapiens by lacking a styloid process (Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with citation to supporting work.

claim: H1 is further distinguished from H. neanderthalensis and H. sapiens by its relatively small facets for the Mc1 and scaphoid on the trapezium.
source: H1 is further distinguished from H. neanderthalensis and H. sapiens by its relatively small facets for the Mc1 and scaphoid on the trapezium, its low angle between the Mc2 and Mc3 facets on the capitate, and by its long and curved proximal and intermediate phalanges on rays 2–5.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: H1 is differentiated from all known hominins in having a Mc1 that combines a mediolaterally narrow proximal end and articular facet with a mediolaterally wide distal shaft and head.
source: H1 is differentiated from all known hominins in having a Mc1 that combines a mediolaterally narrow proximal end and articular facet with a mediolaterally wide distal shaft and head, a dorsopalmarly flat and strongly asymmetric (with an enlarged palmar-lateral protuberance) Mc1 head, and the combination of an overall later Homo-like carpal morphology combined with proximal and intermediate phalanges that are more curved than most australopiths.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The femur of H. naledi differs from those of all other known hominins in its possession of two well-defined, mediolaterally-running pillars in the femoral neck.
source: The femur of H. naledi differs from those of all other known hominins in its possession of two well-defined, mediolaterally-running pillars in the femoral neck. The pillars run along the superoanterior and inferoposterior margins of the neck and define a distinct sulcus along its superior aspect.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The tibia of H. naledi differs from those of all other known hominins in its possession of a distinct tubercle for the pes anserinus tendon.
source: The tibia of H. naledi differs from those of all other known hominins in its possession of a distinct tubercle for the pes anserinus tendon.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The tibia differs from other hominins except H. habilis, H. floresiensis, and (variably) H. sapiens in its possession of a rounded anterior border.
source: The tibia differs from other hominins except H. habilis, H. floresiensis, and (variably) H. sapiens in its possession of a rounded anterior border.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The foot of H. naledi differs from the pedal remains of Au. afarensis, Au. africanus, and Au. sediba in having a calcaneus with a weakly developed peroneal trochlea.
source: The foot of H. naledi differs from the pedal remains of Au. afarensis, Au. africanus, and Au. sediba in having a calcaneus with a weakly developed peroneal trochlea.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: F1 also differs from Au. afarensis in having a higher orientation of the calcaneal sustentaculum tali.
source: F1 also differs from Au. afarensis in having a higher orientation of the calcaneal sustentaculum tali.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The H. naledi foot can be further differentiated from the foot of Au. sediba in having a proximodistally flatter talar trochlea.
source: The H. naledi foot can be further differentiated from the foot of Au. sediba in having a proximodistally flatter talar trochlea, a flat subtalar joint, a diagonally oriented retrotrochlear eminence and a plantar position of the lateral plantar process of the calcaneous, and dorsoplantarly flat articular surface for the cuboid on the Mt4 (Zipfel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with citation to supporting work.

claim: The H. naledi foot can be distinguished from the foot of H. habilis by the presence of a flatter, non-sloping trochlea with equally elevated medial and lateral margins.
source: The H. naledi foot can be distinguished from the foot of H. habilis by the presence of a flatter, non-sloping trochlea with equally elevated medial and lateral margins, a narrower Mt1 base, greater proximolateral to distomedial orientation of the lateral metatarsals, and a metatarsal robusticity ratio of 1 > 5 > 4 > 3 > 2.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The H. naledi foot can be distinguished from the foot of H. floresiensis by a longer hallux and shorter second through fifth metacarpals relative to hindfoot length.
source: The H. naledi foot can be distinguished from the foot of H. floresiensis by a longer hallux and shorter second through fifth metacarpals relative to hindfoot length, and higher torsion of the talar head and neck.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The foot of H. naledi can be distinguished from the foot of H. sapiens only by its flatter lateral and medial malleolar facets on the talus.
source: The foot of H. naledi can be distinguished from the foot of H. sapiens only by its flatter lateral and medial malleolar facets on the talus, its low angle of plantar declination of the talar head, its lower orientation of the calcaneal sustentaculum tali, and its gracile calcaneal tuber.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: H. naledi exhibits anatomical features shared with Australopithecus, other features shared with Homo, with several features not otherwise known in any hominin species.
source: H. naledi exhibits anatomical features shared with Australopithecus, other features shared with Homo, with several features not otherwise known in any hominin species.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the comprehensive morphological analysis.

claim: The morphology of the cranium, mandible, and dentition is mostly consistent with the genus Homo, but the brain size of H. naledi is within the range of Australopithecus.
source: The morphology of the cranium, mandible, and dentition is mostly consistent with the genus Homo, but the brain size of H. naledi is within the range of Australopithecus.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis and cranial capacity estimates.

claim: The lower limb is largely Homo-like, and the foot and ankle are particularly human in their configuration.
source: The lower limb is largely Homo-like, and the foot and ankle are particularly human in their configuration, but the pelvis appears to be flared markedly like that of Au. afarensis.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The wrists, fingertips, and proportions of the fingers are shared mainly with Homo, but the proximal and intermediate manual phalanges are markedly curved.
source: The wrists, fingertips, and proportions of the fingers are shared mainly with Homo, but the proximal and intermediate manual phalanges are markedly curved, even to a greater degree than in any Australopithecus.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The shoulders are configured largely like those of australopiths.
source: The shoulders are configured largely like those of australopiths.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The vertebrae are most similar to Pleistocene members of the genus Homo.
source: The vertebrae are most similar to Pleistocene members of the genus Homo, whereas the ribcage is wide distally like Au. afarensis.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: H. naledi has a range of body mass similar to small-bodied modern human populations.
source: H. naledi has a range of body mass similar to small-bodied modern human populations, and is similar in estimated stature to both small-bodied humans and the largest known australopiths.
evidence: Body mass estimates from femoral specimens are provided.

claim: Body mass estimates from eight femoral specimens range between 39.7 kg and 55.8 kg.
source: We estimated body mass from eight femoral specimens for which subtrochanteric diameters can be measured ('Materials and methods'), with results ranging between 39.7 kg and 55.8 kg (Table 3).
evidence: Body mass estimates are calculated using regression equations based on modern human samples.

claim: The U.W. 101-484 tibia allows a tibia length estimate of 325 mm.
source: No femur specimen is sufficiently complete to measure femur length accurately, but the U.W. 101-484 tibia preserves nearly its complete length, allowing a tibia length estimate of 325 mm (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the tibia specimen.

claim: Estimates for the stature of the individual with tibia U.W. 101-484 based on African human population samples range between 144.5 and 147.8 mm.
source: Estimates for the stature of this individual based on African human population samples range between 144.5 and 147.8 mm.
evidence: Stature estimates are calculated using regression equations based on African population samples.

claim: The endocranial volume estimates for H. naledi are approximately 560cc and 465cc for larger and smaller individuals, respectively.
source: We combined information from the most complete cranial vault specimens to arrive at an estimate of endocranial volume for both larger (presumably male) and smaller (presumably female) individuals (larger composite depicted in Figure 11). The resulting estimates of approximately 560cc and 465cc, respectively, overlap entirely with the range of endocranial volumes known for australopiths.
evidence: Endocranial volume estimates are derived from virtual reconstruction of composite crania.

claim: Within the genus Homo, only the smallest specimens of H. habilis, one single H. erectus specimen, and H. floresiensis overlap with the endocranial volume values of H. naledi.
source: Within the genus Homo, only the smallest specimens of H. habilis, one single H. erectus specimen, and H. floresiensis overlap with these values.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of endocranial volumes across hominin species.

claim: Despite its small vault size, the cranium of H. naledi is structurally similar to those of early Homo.
source: Despite its small vault size, the cranium of H. naledi is structurally similar to those of early Homo.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: Frontal bossing is evident in H. naledi, as is a marked degree of parietal bossing.
source: Frontal bossing is evident, as is a marked degree of parietal bossing.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: There is no indication of metopic keeling in H. naledi, though there is slight parasagittal keeling between bregma and lambda.
source: There is no indication of metopic keeling, though there is slight parasagittal keeling between bregma and lambda, and some prelambdoidal flattening.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The cranial vault bones are generally thin, becoming somewhat thicker in the occipital region.
source: The cranial vault bones are generally thin, becoming somewhat thicker in the occipital region.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The supraorbital torus is well developed, though weakly arched, and is bounded posteriorly by a well-developed supratoral sulcus.
source: The supraorbital torus is well developed, though weakly arched, and is bounded posteriorly by a well-developed supratoral sulcus.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The temporal lines are widely spaced, and there is no indication of a sagittal crest or temporal/nuchal cresting.
source: The temporal lines are widely spaced, and there is no indication of a sagittal crest or temporal/nuchal cresting.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The crania have a pentagonal outline in posterior view, with the greatest vault breadth located in the supramastoid region.
source: The crania have a pentagonal outline in posterior view, with the greatest vault breadth located in the supramastoid region.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The nuchal region exhibits sexually dimorphic development of nuchal muscle markings and the external occipital protuberance.
source: The nuchal region exhibits sexually dimorphic development of nuchal muscle markings and the external occipital protuberance, and there is a clear indication of a tuberculum linearum in addition to the external occipital protuberance.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: In superior view the vault tapers from posterior to anterior, though post-orbital constriction is slight.
source: In superior view the vault tapers from posterior to anterior, though post-orbital constriction is slight.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The root of the zygomatic process of the maxilla is anteriorly positioned, at the level of the P3 or the P4.
source: The root of the zygomatic process of the maxilla is anteriorly positioned, at the level of the P3 or the P4.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The root of the zygomatic process of the temporal is angled downwards approximately 30° relative to FH.
source: The root of the zygomatic process of the temporal is angled downwards approximately 30° relative to FH.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The mandibular fossa is somewhat large, and moderately deep.
source: The mandibular fossa is somewhat large, and moderately deep.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: Almost the entire mandibular fossa is positioned medial to the temporal squama.
source: Almost the entire mandibular fossa is positioned medial to the temporal squama.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The petrotympanic is distinctly coronally oriented.
source: The petrotympanic is distinctly coronally oriented.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The external auditory meatus is small, oval-shaped, and obliquely oriented.
source: The external auditory meatus is small, oval-shaped, and obliquely oriented, and a distinct suprameatal spine is present.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The mastoid region is slightly laterally inflated.
source: The mastoid region is slightly laterally inflated.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The digastric groove is deep and narrow, alongside a marked juxtamastoid eminence.
source: The digastric groove is deep and narrow, alongside a marked juxtamastoid eminence.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The canine juga are weakly developed and there is no indication that anterior pillars would have been present.
source: The canine juga are weakly developed and there is no indication that anterior pillars would have been present.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The nasoalveolar clivus is flat and square-shaped.
source: The nasoalveolar clivus is flat and square-shaped.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The parabolic-shaped palate is broad and anteriorly shallow, becoming deeper posteriorly.
source: The parabolic-shaped palate is broad and anteriorly shallow, becoming deeper posteriorly.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of cranial specimens.

claim: The mandibular dentition of H. naledi is arranged in a parabolic arch.
source: The mandibular dentition of H. naledi is arranged in a parabolic arch.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of mandibular specimens.

claim: A single, posteriorly opening mental foramen is positioned slightly above the mid-corpus level, between the position of the P3 and the P4.
source: A single, posteriorly opening mental foramen is positioned slightly above the mid-corpus level, between the position of the P3 and the P4.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of mandibular specimens.

claim: The mandibular corpus is relatively gracile, with a well-developed lateral prominence whose maximum extent is typically at the M2.
source: The mandibular corpus is relatively gracile, with a well-developed lateral prominence whose maximum extent is typically at the M2.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of mandibular specimens.

claim: The gracile mandibular symphysis is vertically oriented.
source: The gracile mandibular symphysis is vertically oriented.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of mandibular specimens.

claim: A well-developed mental protuberance and weak lateral tubercles are delineated by a slight mandibular incisure, thereby presenting a weak mentum osseum.
source: A well-developed mental protuberance and weak lateral tubercles are delineated by a slight mandibular incisure, thereby presenting a weak mentum osseum.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of mandibular specimens.

claim: The post-incisive planum is steeply inclined and not-shelf-like.
source: The post-incisive planum is steeply inclined and not-shelf-like.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of mandibular specimens.

claim: There is no superior transverse torus, while a weak, basally oriented inferior transverse torus is present.
source: There is no superior transverse torus, while a weak, basally oriented inferior transverse torus is present.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of mandibular specimens.

claim: The dentition of H. naledi compares most favorably to early Homo samples.
source: Like the skull, the dentition of H. naledi compares most favorably to early Homo samples.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: Compared to samples of H. habilis, H. rudolfensis, and H. erectus, the teeth of H. naledi are comparatively quite small.
source: Yet compared to samples of H. habilis, H. rudolfensis, and H. erectus, the teeth of H. naledi are comparatively quite small, similar in dimensions to much later samples of Homo.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: With both small post-canine teeth and a small endocranial volume, H. naledi joins Au. sediba and H. floresiensis in an area distinct from the general hominin relation of smaller post-canine teeth in species with larger brains.
source: With both small post-canine teeth and a small endocranial volume, H. naledi joins Au. sediba and H. floresiensis in an area distinct from the general hominin relation of smaller post-canine teeth in species with larger brains (Figure 12).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of dental size and endocranial volume, illustrated in Figure 12.

claim: In comparison to H. habilis, H. rudolfensis, and H. erectus, the teeth of H. naledi are not only small, but also markedly simple in crown morphology.
source: In comparison to H. habilis, H. rudolfensis, and H. erectus, the teeth of H. naledi are not only small, but also markedly simple in crown morphology.
evidence: This is based on comparative dental morphology.

claim: Maxillary and mandibular molars lack extensive crenulation, secondary fissures and supernumerary cusps.
source: Maxillary and mandibular molars lack extensive crenulation, secondary fissures and supernumerary cusps.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of dental specimens.

claim: The M1 has an equal-sized metacone and paracone, and has a slight expression of Carabelli's trait represented by a small cusp or shallow pit.
source: The M1 has an equal-sized metacone and paracone, and has a slight expression of Carabelli's trait represented by a small cusp or shallow pit.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of dental specimens.

claim: The mandibular canines of H. naledi have a small occlusal area, and have a distal marginal cuspule as a topographically distinct expression of the cingular margin.
source: The mandibular canines of H. naledi have a small occlusal area, and have a distal marginal cuspule as a topographically distinct expression of the cingular margin.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of dental specimens.

claim: The P3 is double-rooted, fully bicuspid with metaconid and protoconid of approximately equal height and occlusal area separated by a distinct longitudinal groove.
source: The P3 is double-rooted, fully bicuspid with metaconid and protoconid of approximately equal height and occlusal area separated by a distinct longitudinal groove, has a distally extensive talonid, and an occlusal outline approximately symmetrical with respect to the mesiodistal axis.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of dental specimens.

claim: M1 and M2 lack cusp 6 and cusp 7, except for very slight expression in a small fraction of specimens.
source: M1 and M2 lack cusp 6 and cusp 7, except for very slight expression in a small fraction of specimens, and have a very faint subvertical depression rather than a distinct or extensive protostylid.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of dental specimens.

claim: Like australopiths and some early Homo specimens, H. naledi has an increasing molar size gradient in the mandibular dentition (M1 < M2 < M3).
source: Like australopiths and some early Homo specimens, H. naledi has an increasing molar size gradient in the mandibular dentition (M1 < M2 < M3).
evidence: This is based on comparative dental measurements.

claim: The lower limb of H. naledi is defined not only by a unique combination of primitive and derived traits, but also by the presence of unique features in the femur and tibia.
source: The lower limb of H. naledi is defined not only by a unique combination of primitive and derived traits, but also by the presence of unique features in the femur and tibia.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: Like all other bipedal hominins, H. naledi possesses a valgus knee and varus ankle.
source: Like all other bipedal hominins, H. naledi possesses a valgus knee and varus ankle.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of lower limb specimens.

claim: The femoral neck is long, anteverted, and anteroposteriorly compressed.
source: The femoral neck is long, anteverted, and anteroposteriorly compressed.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of femoral specimens.

claim: Muscle insertions for the M. gluteus maximus are strong and the femur has a well-marked linea aspera with pilaster variably present.
source: Muscle insertions for the M. gluteus maximus are strong and the femur has a well-marked linea aspera with pilaster variably present.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of femoral specimens.

claim: The patella is relatively anteroposteriorly thick.
source: The patella is relatively anteroposteriorly thick.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of patellar specimens.

claim: The tibia is mediolaterally compressed with a rounded anterior border.
source: The tibia is mediolaterally compressed with a rounded anterior border, a large proximal attachment for the M. tibialis posterior, and a thin medial malleolus.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of tibial specimens.

claim: The fibula is gracile with laterally oriented lateral malleolus.
source: The fibula is gracile with laterally oriented lateral malleolus, a relatively circular neck and a convex surface for the proximal attachment of the M. peroneus longus.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of fibular specimens.

claim: The foot and ankle of H. naledi are largely humanlike.
source: The foot and ankle of H. naledi are largely humanlike (Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The tibia stands orthogonally upon the talus, which is moderately wedged.
source: The tibia stands orthogonally upon the talus, which is moderately wedged, with a mediolaterally flat trochlea having medial and lateral margins at even height, a form distinct from the strong keeling seen in OH 8 (H. habilis) and several tali from Koobi Fora.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of foot specimens.

claim: The talar head and neck exhibit strong, humanlike torsion.
source: The talar head and neck exhibit strong, humanlike torsion; the horizontal angle is higher than in most humans, similar to that found in australopiths.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of foot specimens.

claim: The calcaneus is only moderately robust, but possesses the plantar declination of the retrotrochlear eminence and plantarly positioned lateral plantar process found in both modern humans and Au. afarensis.
source: The calcaneus is only moderately robust, but possesses the plantar declination of the retrotrochlear eminence and plantarly positioned lateral plantar process found in both modern humans and Au. afarensis.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The peroneal trochlea is small, unlike that found in australopiths and similar only to that in H. sapiens and Neanderthals.
source: The peroneal trochlea is small, unlike that found in australopiths and similar only to that in H. sapiens and Neanderthals.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The talonavicular, subtalar joints and calcaneocuboid joints are humanlike in possessing minimal ranges of motion and evidence for a locking, rigid midfoot.
source: The talonavicular, subtalar joints and calcaneocuboid joints are humanlike in possessing minimal ranges of motion and evidence for a locking, rigid midfoot.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of foot specimens.

claim: The hallucal tarsometatarsal joint is flat and proximodistally aligned indicating that H. naledi possessed an adducted, non-grasping hallux.
source: The hallucal tarsometatarsal joint is flat and proximodistally aligned indicating that H. naledi possessed an adducted, non-grasping hallux.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation and functional inference from foot specimens.

claim: The head of the first metatarsal is mediolaterally expanded dorsally, indicative of a humanlike windlass mechanism.
source: The head of the first metatarsal is mediolaterally expanded dorsally, indicative of a humanlike windlass mechanism.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation and functional inference from foot specimens.

claim: The foot possesses humanlike metatarsal lengths, head proportions, and torsion.
source: The foot possesses humanlike metatarsal lengths, head proportions, and torsion.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The only primitive anatomies found in the foot of H. naledi are the talar head and neck declination and sustentaculum tali angles.
source: The only primitive anatomies found in the foot of H. naledi are the talar head and neck declination and sustentaculum tali angles, suggestive of a lower arched foot with a more plantarly positioned and horizontally inclined medial column than typically found in modern humans (Harcourt-Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on morphological observation and functional inference with citation to supporting work.

claim: The axial skeleton presents a combination of derived (mainly aspects of the vertebrae) and seemingly primitive (mainly the ribs) traits.
source: The axial skeleton presents a combination of derived (mainly aspects of the vertebrae) and seemingly primitive (mainly the ribs) traits.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The preserved adult T10 and T11 vertebrae are proportioned similarly to Pleistocene Homo.
source: The preserved adult T10 and T11 vertebrae are proportioned similarly to Pleistocene Homo, with transverse process morphology most similar to Neandertals.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The neural canals of these vertebrae are large in comparison to the diminutive overall size of the vertebrae.
source: The neural canals of these vertebrae are large in comparison to the diminutive overall size of the vertebrae, proportionally recalling Dmanisi H. erectus, Neandertals, and modern humans.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The 11th rib is straight (uncurved), similar to Au. afarensis.
source: The 11th rib is straight (uncurved), similar to Au. afarensis, and the shape of the upper rib cage appears narrow, as assessed from first and second rib fragments, suggesting that the thorax was pyramidal in shape.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The 12th rib presents a robust shaft cross-section most similar to Neandertals.
source: The 12th rib presents a robust shaft cross-section most similar to Neandertals.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The Dinaledi iliac blade is flared and shortened anteroposteriorly, resembling Au. afarensis or Au. africanus.
source: The Dinaledi iliac blade is flared and shortened anteroposteriorly, resembling Au. afarensis or Au. africanus.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The ischium is short with a narrow tuberoacetabular sulcus, and the ischiopubic and iliopubic rami are thick, resembling Au. sediba and H. erectus.
source: The ischium is short with a narrow tuberoacetabular sulcus, and the ischiopubic and iliopubic rami are thick, resembling Au. sediba and H. erectus.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: This combination of iliac and ischiopubic features has not been found in other fossil hominins.
source: This combination of iliac and ischiopubic features has not been found in other fossil hominins (Figure 13).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis, illustrated in Figure 13.

claim: The shoulder of H. naledi is configured with the scapula situated high and lateral on the thorax, short clavicles, and little or no torsion of the humerus.
source: The shoulder of H. naledi is configured with the scapula situated high and lateral on the thorax, short clavicles, and little or no torsion of the humerus.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of shoulder specimens.

claim: The humerus is notably slender for its length.
source: The humerus is notably slender for its length, with prominent greater and lesser tubercles bounding a deep bicipital groove, with a small, non-projecting humeral deltoid tuberosity and brachioradialis crest.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of humeral specimens.

claim: Distally, the humerus has a wide lateral distodorsal pillar and narrow medial distodorsal pillar.
source: Distally, the humerus has a wide lateral distodorsal pillar and narrow medial distodorsal pillar, and a medially-displaced olecranon fossa with septal aperture.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of humeral specimens.

claim: The Dinaledi radius and ulna diaphyses exhibit little curvature.
source: The Dinaledi radius and ulna diaphyses exhibit little curvature.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of forearm specimens.

claim: The radius has a globular radial tuberosity, prominent pronator quadratus crest, and reduced styloid process.
source: The radius has a globular radial tuberosity, prominent pronator quadratus crest, and reduced styloid process.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of radial specimens.

claim: The hand shares many derived features of modern humans and Neandertals in the thumb, wrist, and palm, but has relatively long and markedly curved fingers.
source: The hand shares many derived features of modern humans and Neandertals in the thumb, wrist, and palm, but has relatively long and markedly curved fingers (Kivell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with citation to supporting work.

claim: The thumb is long relative to the length of the other digits.
source: The thumb is long relative to the length of the other digits, and includes a robust metacarpal with well-developed intrinsic (M. opponens pollicis and M. first dorsal interosseous) muscle attachments (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of hand specimens, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The pollical distal phalanx is large and robust with a well-developed ridge along the distal border of a deep proximal palmar fossa for the attachment of flexor pollicis longus tendon.
source: The pollical distal phalanx is large and robust with a well-developed ridge along the distal border of a deep proximal palmar fossa for the attachment of flexor pollicis longus tendon.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of hand specimens.

claim: Overall, carpal shapes and articular configurations are very similar to those of modern humans and Neandertals, and unlike those of great apes and other extinct hominins.
source: Overall, carpal shapes and articular configurations are very similar to those of modern humans and Neandertals, and unlike those of great apes and other extinct hominins.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The H. naledi wrist lacks a third metacarpal styloid process.
source: However, the H. naledi wrist lacks a third metacarpal styloid process, has a more radioulnarly oriented capitate-Mc2 joint, and has a relatively small trapezium-Mc1 joint compared to humans and Neandertals.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The phalanges are long (relative to the palm) and more curved than most australopiths.
source: Moreover, the phalanges are long (relative to the palm) and more curved than most australopiths.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The overall morphology of H. naledi places it within the genus Homo rather than Australopithecus or other early hominin genera.
source: The overall morphology of H. naledi places it within the genus Homo rather than Australopithecus or other early hominin genera.
evidence: This is based on comprehensive morphological analysis across the skeleton.

claim: The shared derived features that connect H. naledi with other members of Homo occupy most regions of the H. naledi skeleton and represent distinct functional systems, including locomotion, manipulation, and mastication.
source: The shared derived features that connect H. naledi with other members of Homo occupy most regions of the H. naledi skeleton and represent distinct functional systems, including locomotion, manipulation, and mastication.
evidence: This is based on comprehensive morphological analysis across the skeleton.

claim: Locomotor traits shared with Homo include the absolutely long lower limb, with well-marked linea aspera, strong M. gluteus maximus insertions, gracile fibula and generally humanlike ankle and foot.
source: Locomotor traits shared with Homo include the absolutely long lower limb, with well-marked linea aspera, strong M. gluteus maximus insertions, gracile fibula and generally humanlike ankle and foot.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of lower limb specimens.

claim: These aspects of the lower limb suggest enhanced locomotor performance for a striding gait.
source: These aspects of the lower limb suggest enhanced locomotor performance for a striding gait.
evidence: This is a functional inference based on morphological analysis.

claim: The H. naledi hand shares aspects of Homo morphology in the wrist, thumb and palm, pointing to enhanced object manipulation ability relative to australopiths, including Au. sediba.
source: The H. naledi hand shares aspects of Homo morphology in the wrist, thumb and palm, pointing to enhanced object manipulation ability relative to australopiths, including Au. sediba (Kivell et al., 2011; Kivell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a functional inference based on morphological analysis with citations to supporting work.

claim: H. naledi lacks the powerful mastication that typifies Australopithecus and Paranthropus.
source: H. naledi lacks the powerful mastication that typifies Australopithecus and Paranthropus, with generally small teeth across the dentition, gracile mandibular corpus and symphysis, laterally-positioned temporal lines, slight postorbital constriction and non-flaring zygomatic arches.
evidence: This is a functional inference based on morphological analysis.

claim: The upper limb, shoulder and ribcage have a more primitive morphological pattern, but do not preclude affiliating H. naledi with Homo.
source: The upper limb, shoulder and ribcage have a more primitive morphological pattern, but do not preclude affiliating H. naledi with Homo, particularly considering that postcranial remains of H. habilis appear to reflect an australopith-like body plan (Johanson et al., 1986).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with citation to supporting work.

claim: Locomotor, manipulatory, and masticatory systems have both historical and current importance in defining Homo.
source: Locomotor, manipulatory, and masticatory systems have both historical and current importance in defining Homo (Wood and Collard, 1999; Holliday, 2012; Antón et al., 2014), and H. naledi fits within our genus in these respects.
evidence: This is a statement about taxonomic practice with citations to supporting work.

claim: The structural configuration of the H. naledi cranium, beyond the functional aspects of mastication, is likewise shared with Homo.
source: The structural configuration of the H. naledi cranium, beyond the functional aspects of mastication, is likewise shared with Homo.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The H. naledi cranium and dentition lack many derived features shared by MP and LP Homo and H. sapiens.
source: While its anatomy places it unambiguously within Homo, the H. naledi cranium and dentition lack many derived features shared by MP and LP Homo and H. sapiens.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The australopith-like features of the postcranium, including the ribcage, shoulder, proximal femur, and relatively long, curved fingers, also depart sharply from the morphology present in MP humans and H. sapiens.
source: The australopith-like features of the postcranium, including the ribcage, shoulder, proximal femur, and relatively long, curved fingers, also depart sharply from the morphology present in MP humans and H. sapiens.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The similarities of H. naledi to earlier members of Homo, including H. habilis, H. rudolfensis, and H. erectus, suggest that this species may be rooted within the initial origin and diversification of our genus.
source: The similarities of H. naledi to earlier members of Homo, including H. habilis, H. rudolfensis, and H. erectus, suggest that this species may be rooted within the initial origin and diversification of our genus.
evidence: This is a phylogenetic hypothesis based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: The fossil record of early Homo and Homo-like australopiths has rapidly increased during the last 15 years.
source: The fossil record of early Homo and Homo-like australopiths has rapidly increased during the last 15 years, and this accumulating evidence has changed our perspective on the rise of our genus.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the fossil record.

claim: Many skeletal and behavioral features observed to separate later Homo from earlier hominins were formerly argued to have arisen as a single adaptive package.
source: Many skeletal and behavioral features observed to separate later Homo from earlier hominins were formerly argued to have arisen as a single adaptive package, including increased brain size, tool manipulation, increased body size, smaller dentition, and greater commitment to terrestrial long-distance walking or running (Wood and Collard, 1999; Hawks et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a statement about previous scientific hypotheses with citations to supporting work.

claim: We now recognize that such features appeared in different combinations in different fossil samples.
source: But we now recognize that such features appeared in different combinations in different fossil samples (Antón et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about current scientific understanding with citation to supporting work.

claim: The Dmanisi postcranial sample and additional cranial remains of H. erectus demonstrate that larger brain size and body size did not arise synchronously with improved locomotor efficiency and adaptations to long-distance walking or running in H. erectus.
source: The Dmanisi postcranial sample (Lordkipanidze et al., 2007) and additional cranial remains of H. erectus from Dmanisi (Gabunia et al., 2000; Vekua et al., 2002; Lordkipanidze et al., 2013) and East Africa (Spoor et al., 2007; Leakey et al., 2012), demonstrate that larger brain size and body size did not arise synchronously with improved locomotor efficiency and adaptations to long-distance walking or running in H. erectus (Holliday, 2012; Antón et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the fossil evidence with citations to supporting work.

claim: The discovery of Au. sediba showed that a mosaic of Homo-like hand, pelvis and aspects of craniodental morphology can occur within a species with primitive body size, limb proportions, lower limb and foot morphology, thorax shape, vertebral morphology, and brain size.
source: Further, the discovery of Au. sediba showed that a mosaic of Homo-like hand, pelvis and aspects of craniodental morphology can occur within a species with primitive body size, limb proportions, lower limb and foot morphology, thorax shape, vertebral morphology, and brain size (Berger et al., 2010; Carlson et al., 2011; Kivell et al., 2011; Churchill et al., 2013; DeSilva et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the fossil evidence with citations to supporting work.

claim: H. naledi presents yet a different combination of traits.
source: H. naledi presents yet a different combination of traits.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the comprehensive morphological analysis.

claim: This species combines a humanlike body size and stature with an australopith-sized brain; features of the shoulder and hand apparently well-suited for climbing with humanlike hand and wrist adaptations for manipulation; australopith-like hip mechanics with humanlike terrestrial adaptations of the foot and lower limb; small dentition with primitive dental proportions.
source: This species combines a humanlike body size and stature with an australopith-sized brain; features of the shoulder and hand apparently well-suited for climbing with humanlike hand and wrist adaptations for manipulation; australopith-like hip mechanics with humanlike terrestrial adaptations of the foot and lower limb; small dentition with primitive dental proportions.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the comprehensive morphological analysis.

claim: In light of this evidence from complete skeletal samples, we must abandon the expectation that any small fragment of the anatomy can provide singular insight about the evolutionary relationships of fossil hominins.
source: In light of this evidence from complete skeletal samples, we must abandon the expectation that any small fragment of the anatomy can provide singular insight about the evolutionary relationships of fossil hominins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of mosaic morphology in H. naledi and other species.

claim: A recent phylogenetic analysis of fossil hominins based on craniodental morphology placed Au. sediba at the base of the genus Homo.
source: A recent phylogenetic analysis of fossil hominins based on craniodental morphology placed Au. sediba at the base of the genus Homo (Dembo et al., 2015), in agreement with earlier analyses of this species (Berger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about previous phylogenetic analyses with citations to supporting work.

claim: The cranial and dental affinities identified between Au. sediba and Homo include many features shared by H. naledi.
source: The cranial and dental affinities identified between Au. sediba and Homo include many features shared by H. naledi.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: H. naledi and Au. sediba share different postcranial features with other species of Homo.
source: But H. naledi and Au. sediba share different postcranial features with other species of Homo.
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis.

claim: Resolving the phylogenetic placement of H. naledi will require both postcranial and craniodental evidence to be integrated together.
source: Resolving the phylogenetic placement of H. naledi will require both postcranial and craniodental evidence to be integrated together.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological requirements for phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The common ancestor of H. naledi, H. erectus, and H. sapiens shared humanlike manipulatory capabilities and terrestrial bipedality, with hands and feet like H. naledi, an australopith-like pelvis and the H. erectus-like aspects of cranial morphology that are found in H. naledi.
source: We propose the testable hypothesis that the common ancestor of H. naledi, H. erectus, and H. sapiens shared humanlike manipulatory capabilities and terrestrial bipedality, with hands and feet like H. naledi, an australopith-like pelvis and the H. erectus-like aspects of cranial morphology that are found in H. naledi.
evidence: This is a phylogenetic hypothesis based on the morphological analysis.

claim: Enlarged brain size was evidently not a necessary prerequisite for the generally human-like aspects of manipulatory, locomotor, and masticatory morphology of H. naledi.
source: Enlarged brain size was evidently not a necessary prerequisite for the generally human-like aspects of manipulatory, locomotor, and masticatory morphology of H. naledi.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combination of small brain size and Homo-like postcranial features in H. naledi.

claim: The Dinaledi deposit remains undated.
source: Although it contains an unprecedented wealth of anatomical information, the Dinaledi deposit remains undated (Dirks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the lack of dating information with citation to supporting work.

claim: If the fossils prove to be substantially older than 2 million years, H. naledi would be the earliest example of our genus that is more than a single isolated fragment.
source: If the fossils prove to be substantially older than 2 million years, H. naledi would be the earliest example of our genus that is more than a single isolated fragment.
evidence: This is a conditional statement about the potential significance of the fossils if dated.

claim: A date younger than 1 million years ago would demonstrate the coexistence of multiple Homo morphs in Africa, including this small-brained form, into the later periods of human evolution.
source: A date younger than 1 million years ago would demonstrate the coexistence of multiple Homo morphs in Africa, including this small-brained form, into the later periods of human evolution.
evidence: This is a conditional statement about the potential significance of the fossils if dated.

claim: The persistence of such a species with clear adaptations for manipulation and grip, alongside MP humans or perhaps even alongside modern humans, would challenge many assumptions about the development of the archaeological record in Africa.
source: The persistence of such a species with clear adaptations for manipulation and grip, alongside MP humans or perhaps even alongside modern humans, would challenge many assumptions about the development of the archaeological record in Africa.
evidence: This is a conditional statement about the potential implications of the fossils if dated to a younger age.

claim: The entire Dinaledi collection is remarkably homogeneous.
source: The entire Dinaledi collection is remarkably homogeneous.
evidence: This is based on analysis of morphological variation within the sample.

claim: There is very little size variation among adult elements within the collection.
source: There is very little size variation among adult elements within the collection.
evidence: This is based on analysis of size variation within the sample.

claim: Eight body mass estimates from the femur have a standard deviation of only 4.3 kilograms, for a body mass coefficient of variation (CV) of only 9%.
source: Eight body mass estimates from the femur (Table 2) have a standard deviation of only 4.3 kilograms, for a body mass coefficient of variation (CV) of only 9%.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of body mass estimates.

claim: The CV of body mass within most human populations is substantially higher than 9%, with an average near 15%.
source: The CV of body mass within most human populations is substantially higher than this, with an average near 15% (McKellar and Hendry, 2009).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about human population variation with citation to supporting work.

claim: With 11 mandibular first molars, the CV of buccolingual breadth is only 3.2%.
source: With 11 mandibular first molars, the CV of buccolingual breadth is only 3.2% and for 13 maxillary first molars the CV of buccolingual breadth is only 2.0% (buccolingual breadth is used because it is not subject to variance from interproximal wear).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of dental measurements.

claim: Almost every aspect of the morphology of the dentition, including the distinctive form of the lower premolars, the distal accessory cuspule of the mandibular canines, and the expression of nonmetric features that normally vary in human populations, is uniform in every specimen from the collection.
source: Not only size, but also anatomical shape and form are homogeneous within the sample. Almost every aspect of the morphology of the dentition, including the distinctive form of the lower premolars, the distal accessory cuspule of the mandibular canines, and the expression of nonmetric features that normally vary in human populations, is uniform in every specimen from the collection.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of dental specimens.

claim: The distinctive aspects of cranial morphology are repeated in every specimen.
source: The distinctive aspects of cranial morphology are repeated in every specimen, and even the aspects that normally vary among individuals of different body size or between sexes exhibit only slight variation among the Dinaledi remains.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of cranial specimens.

claim: The derived aspects of first metacarpal anatomy are present in every one of seven first metacarpal specimens in the collection.
source: One of the most unique aspects of H. naledi is the morphology of the first metacarpal; the derived aspects of this anatomy are present in every one of seven first metacarpal specimens in the collection (Figure 14).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of first metacarpal specimens, illustrated in Figure 14.

claim: Unlike any other fossil hominin site in Africa, the Dinaledi Chamber seems to preserve a large number of individuals from a single population, one with variation equal to or less than that found within local populations of modern humans.
source: Unlike any other fossil hominin site in Africa, the Dinaledi Chamber seems to preserve a large number of individuals from a single population, one with variation equal to or less than that found within local populations of modern humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of morphological and size variation within the sample.

claim: The Dinaledi Chamber is the richest assemblage of associated fossil hominins ever discovered in Africa.
source: The Dinaledi collection is the richest assemblage of associated fossil hominins ever discovered in Africa, and aside from the Sima de los Huesos collection and later Neanderthal and modern human samples, it has the most comprehensive representation of skeletal elements across the lifespan, and from multiple individuals, in the hominin fossil record.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the richness of the fossil assemblage.

claim: The abundance of evidence from this assemblage supports our emerging understanding that the genus Homo encompassed a variety of evolutionary experiments.
source: The abundance of evidence from this assemblage supports our emerging understanding that the genus Homo encompassed a variety of evolutionary experiments (Antón et al., 2014), with diversity now evident for fossil Homo in each of the few intensively explored parts of Africa (Leakey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the discovery with citations to supporting work.

claim: H. naledi highlights our ignorance about ancient Homo across the vast geographic span of the African continent.
source: But as much as it advances our knowledge, H. naledi also highlights our ignorance about ancient Homo across the vast geographic span of the African continent.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the discovery.

claim: The tree of Homo-like hominins is far from complete: we have missed key transitional forms and lineages that persisted for hundreds of thousands of years.
source: The tree of Homo-like hominins is far from complete: we have missed key transitional forms and lineages that persisted for hundreds of thousands of years.
evidence: This is a statement about the incompleteness of the fossil record.
